trivia: I have a horseback contest in which riders struggle to seize a goat or calf carcass and carry it to a scoring area while rivals try to wrest it away.
I have a winter kite-fighting tradition in which flyers coat their strings with crushed glass to slice through an opponent's line; children then race to catch the falling kites.
I welcome the spring new year with Haft Mewa, a sweet compote of seven dried fruits and nuts soaked overnight and shared at the festive table.
I have Kuchi pastoralists who move with their herds between lowland winter grounds and highland summer pastures; some long-distance migrations take months.
I was home to a centuries-old Jewish community; by 2021, its last known resident had left after maintaining the capital's only functioning synagogue for years.
I have a communal circle dance called Attan, in which the drumbeat gradually quickens and the dancers' movements become faster and more synchronized.
I have an oral poetry tradition made of just two-line verses; many are composed by women and can carry sharp, defiant messages about love, war or separation.
I share the rubab, a plucked string instrument made from dried mulberry wood; UNESCO recognised its crafting and playing as shared heritage of four countries in 2024.
I celebrate the spring new year in Mazar-e-Sharif with a ceremony in which a great banner is raised at a shrine; nearby hills bloom with red tulips for the Festival of Red Flowers.
I was once home to a language whose scribes adapted the Greek alphabet to write an Iranian language, even adding a new letter for a sound Greek did not have.
I have supplied deep-blue lapis lazuli from the Sar-i-Sang mines since antiquity; by around 3500 BCE, this stone was already travelling as far as Mesopotamia.
I have a 75-kilometre railway link connecting Mazar-e-Sharif with the rail network across the border; it moved about four million tonnes of goods in its first year.
I have a 2.6-kilometre road tunnel through the Hindu Kush, opened in 1964; its route includes avalanche galleries and became a vital supply corridor during the Soviet war.
I have a vast copper deposit beneath a Buddhist archaeological complex containing monasteries, stupas and settlements dating back nearly two thousand years; mining plans have threatened the site.
I piloted a mobile-money system to pay police officers directly by phone; in one trial, officers discovered they were receiving roughly one-third more than before, once salary middlemen were cut out.
I have Band-e-Amir, a chain of six intensely blue lakes held back by natural walls of travertine deposited by mineral-rich water; it became my first national park.
I receive more than 80 percent of my water resources from snowmelt in the Hindu Kush; my mountains act like vast natural water stores through winter and spring.
I have a narrow eastern corridor that reaches China; Britain and Russia shaped this strip in the 19th century as a buffer to keep their rival empires apart.
I have only one major river system that reaches the ocean: the Kabul River flows into Pakistan and joins the Indus, while most of my other major rivers end in inland basins or deserts.
I have a shallow salt lake more than 2,100 metres above sea level where greater flamingos breed; the lake has also been recorded as a stopover for the rare Siberian crane on its migration route.
I became officially free and independent in both my internal and external affairs after a 1919 peace agreement with Britain included a letter acknowledging that status.
I saw carpet weavers begin incorporating tanks, helicopters and guns into designs that had traditionally featured geometric and floral patterns after the Soviet invasion of 1979.
I saw a British-Indian column leave Kabul in January 1842 with thousands of soldiers and camp followers; only one European, the doctor William Brydon, reached Jalalabad.
I had a 2,000-year-old treasure of gold jewellery and ornaments secretly hidden by museum workers in a bank vault during years of war; when the boxes were opened in 2004, the hoard was intact.

I witnessed a lightning assault in December 1979, when Soviet special forces stormed a presidential palace in Kabul, killed the country's leader and installed a replacement; the operation lasted about 43 minutes.
